κεκίνησθε εἰς τὸ ἐρεθίσαι με. Ὄμνυμι δὲ ὑμῖν, καὶ ὄμνυμι κατὰ τοῦ ζῶντος Κυρίου
αὐτοῦ, κρίναντός με ταῦτα παθεῖν, αὐτοῦ τοῦ παραδόντος με ταύταις περιστάσεσι,
τοῦ δόντος ἐξουσίαν τῷ διαβόλῳ τοιούτοις με ἐξετασμοῖς ἐξετάζεσθαι, καὶ
βασανίζεσθαι. Ὄμνυμι κατὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, καί φημι, ὅτι ζῇ Κύριος, ὃς οὕτω με κέκρικε,
καὶ ὁ Παντο κράτωρ, ὁ παραπικράνας μου τὴν ψυχήν. Στίχ. εʹ. Μή μοι εἴη δικαίους
ὑμᾶς ἀποφῆναι, ἕως ἂν ἀποθάνω. Ἐὰν συγκαταθῶμεν οἷς λέγετε, ὅτι νενοήκατε διὰ
τί ταῦτα πέπονθα, δικαίους ὑμᾶς ἀπεφηνάμην ἕως ἂν ἀποθάνω. Στίχ. εʹ. Οὐ γὰρ
ἀπαλλάξω τὴν ἀκακίαν μου. Οὐκ ἀφήσω τὸ προσέχειν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ· μεμνή σομαι
ἀεὶ περιέχεσθαι αὐτῆς. Στίχ. ʹ. Οὐ γὰρ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ ἄτοπα πρᾶξαι. Πολλὴ ἡ
παῤῥησία αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ προτέρῳ βίῳ, καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς
περιστάσεως, ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν· Οὐ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ ἄτοπα πρᾶξαι. ΚΕΦ. ΚΗʹ. Στίχ.
ιβʹ. Ποῖος δὲ τόπος ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμης; Ἐπιστήμη ἡ περιοχὴ τῶν ὡσαύτως ἐχόντων θεω
ρίᾳ· σύνεσις δὲ ἡ διάκρισις. Στίχ. ιεʹ. Καὶ οὐ σταθήσεται ἀργύριον ἀντάλ λαγμα αὐτῆς.
Οὐδὲν ἀντάξιόν ἐστιν τῆς σοφίας. Ἐὰν ἁπλούστε ρον νοῇς τὸ ἀργύριον καὶ τὸ
χρυσίον, εὐθέως ἐρεῖ Ἰὼβ, ὅτι οὐδὲν ἄξιόν ἐστι τῆς σοφίας. Στίχ. ι ʹ. Ἐν ὄνυχι τιμίῳ
καὶ σαπφείρῳ. Οὐδὲ ὄνυχι τιμίῳ ἡ σοφία παραβληθήσεται· ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ἐν σαπφείρῳ
ἰσωθήσεται αὕτη. Στίχ. ιηʹ. Μετέωρα καὶ γάβεις οὐ μνησθήσεται. Οὐδὲ τὰ μετέωρα
ἄξιά ἐστι τῆς σοφίας, οὐδὲ γά βις. Ἔοικε δὲ ἐπὶ δυναμένων τάχθαι, οἱονεὶ γι
γαρτικῶν. Τινὲς δέ φασιν, ὅτι γάβις λέγεται τὸ ὑπερέχον τοῦ χείλους τοῦ μεδίμνου, ὃ
καλεῖται κομ μουλᾶτον. Στίχ. ιηʹ. Καὶ ἕλκυσον σοφίαν ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσώτατα. Τὰ ἐσώτατα
περὶ τὴν Ἰνδίαν, ἢ τὰ περὶ τὴν ἐπέκεινα χώραν, ἔνθα εἰσὶ τίμιοι λίθοι. Φέρει δὲ
ἐκείνη ἡ χώρα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ταῦτα, νομιζόμενα παρὰ τοῖς πλουσίοις εἶναι
θαυμαστά. Παρ' ἐκεῖνα οὖν τὰ ἐσώτατα ἕλκυσον εἰς σαυτὸν τὴν σοφίαν. Ἢ, ὑπὲρ τὰ
ἐσώτατα, ὑπεραπόῤῥητα τὰ ἔνδον μυστήρια 17.92 τὰ ἅγια τοῦ Θεοῦ· ὑπὲρ πάντα
πολλὰ ὄντα, ἕλκυσον τὴν σοφίαν. Στίχ. καʹ. Λέληθε πάντα ἄνθρωπον. Λέληθε πάντα
ἄνθρωπον, κἂν προφήτης ᾖ, κἂν ἀπόστολος. ΚΕΦ. ΚΘʹ. Στίχ. ʹ. Ὅτε ἐχέοντό μου αἱ
ὁδοὶ βούτυρον. Προειρήκαμεν περὶ τῶν ὁδῶν τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ἃς ὥδευ σεν, ὅτι ἀρεταὶ ἦσαν.
Ἐχέοντο οὖν αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτοῦ βουτύρῳ, ὥδευε τὴν σωφροσύνην, καὶ οἱονεὶ ἐχεῖτο ἡ
σωφροσύνη, ὡς πολλοὺς τρέφεσθαι καὶ τῶν νηπίων ἀπὸ τῆς σωφροσύνης τοῦ Ἰὼβ,
ἀπὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνδρείας. Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν· Ὅτε ἐχέοντο αἱ
ὁδοί μου βουτύρῳ. Στίχ. ʹ. Τὰ δὲ ὄρη μου ἐχέοντο γάλακτι. Ὅσα ἦν ὑψηλὰ νοήματα
καὶ μεγάλα, ταῦτα ἦν ὄρη τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ἐφ' ἃ ἀνέβαινεν. Στίχ. ζʹ. Ὅτε ἐξεπορευόμην
ὄρθιος ἐν πόλει. ∆ιδασκαλίᾳ ἐσχόλαζε καὶ ὠφελείᾳ, ἐρῶν, οὐχ ὡς φίλαυτος, ἀλλ' ὡς
ἀγάπην ἔχων ζητοῦσαν τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον. Στίχ. θʹ. ∆άκτυλον ἐπιθέντες ἐπὶ
στόματι. ∆όξει μὲν οὖν καὶ σημεῖον εἶναι τὸ, ∆άκτυλον ἐπι θέντες ἐπὶ στόματι
αὐτῶν, σιωπῆς. Τάχα δὲ δηλοῖ, ἐπεὶ ἡ χεὶρ ἀντὶ ἔργων λαμβάνεται, ὡς πολλάκις ἐδεί
ξαμεν, ὅτι τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν ἐπέθηκαν ἐπὶ στόμα, αἰσθανθέντες ἐν ὀλίγῳ ἔργῳ, ὅτι οὐκ
εἰσὶν ἄξιοι τοῦ λαλεῖν, παρόντος τοῦ Ἰὼβ, μείζονα ἔργα πε ποιηκότος. Στίχ. ιʹ. Οἱ δὲ
ἀκούσαντες ἐμακάρισάν με. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Τοσοῦτον ἦν ὅτε οὐδέπω ἐβασανίζετο, ὥστε
οἱ ἀκούοντες αὐτοῦ ἐμακάριζον αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐθαύ μαζον, τίνα τρόπον τὰ τοσαῦτα νοεῖ
καὶ καταλαμβά νει, καὶ δύναται τοὺς ἀκούοντας ὠφελεῖν. Στίχ. ιʹ. Ὅτι γλῶσσα
αὐτῶν τῷ λάρυγγι αὐτῶν ἐκολλήθη. Τῶν ἀκουόντων μου καὶ μακαριζόντων ἐφ' οἷς
ἔλε γον, ἡ γλῶσσα τῷ λάρυγγι ἐκολλήθη. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Ὅτι ὠτίον ἤκουσε, καὶ ἐμακάρισέ
με. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Ὥσπερ γέγραπται περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως, ὅτι ηὐλαβεῖτο κατεμβλέψαι
κατενώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τὴν ὑπερβολὴν τῆς λαμπρότητος αὐτοῦ οὕτως νοήσας ἂν,
ὅτι ὑπερβολὴ ἦν προκοπῆς τῆς ἐν σοφίᾳ τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ὥστε τοὺς ἀκούοντας αὐτοῦ μὴ δύ
νασθαι ἐνορᾷν τῇ μαρμαρυγῇ τῶν νοημάτων αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ δυναμένους διὰ τοῦτο
ἐκκλίνειν τοὺς ὀφθαλ μοὺς αὐτῶν, μὴ παρακολουθοῦντας τῇ βαθυτάτῃ τῆς διανοίας
αὐτοῦ. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο λέγει· Στίχ. ιαʹ. Ὀφθαλμὸς δέ με ἰδὼν ἐξέκλινεν. Ὁ μὲν Ἀκύλας καὶ
Σύμμαχος, Ἐμαρτύρησε περὶ ἐμοῦ, ἐκδεδώκασιν· ἕτεροι δὲ, Ὀφθαλμὸς δὲ ἰδὼν
ἐξέκλινεν, ἀντὶ τοῦ· Οὐκ ἰσχύω ἀντειπεῖν. 17.93 Στίχ. ιβʹ. ∆ιέσωσα γὰρ πτωχὸν ἐκ
χειρὸς δυ νάστου. Ἴδωμεν αὐτοῦ τὰ ἀνδραγαθήματα, καὶ ἁπλώσω μεν. Καὶ κατὰ τὸ
ῥητὸν ἔχει λόγον τοῦτο, καὶ κατ' ἀναγωγὴν ἔχει πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἑρμηνείαν. Κατὰ τὸ
pass_a_gloss: …you have been moved to provoke me. I swear to you, and I swear by the living Lord himself, the one who judged me to suffer these things, himself the one who handed me over to these circumstances, the one who gave authority to the devil that I be examined with such examinations, and be tortured. I swear by the Lord, and I say that the Lord lives, who has thus judged me, and the Almighty, the one who embittered my soul. Verse 5. May it not be for me to declare you righteous until I die. If we assent to the things you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I declared you righteous until I die. Verse 5. For I will not remove my innocence. I will not let go of attending to righteousness; I will remember always to be held by it. Verse 6 (numeral lost in the print). For I am not conscious with myself of having done out-of-place things. Much is his freedom of speech both upon the former life and upon the things at the time of the trouble, so that he says: I am not conscious with myself of having done out-of-place things. Chapter 28, verse 12. But what sort of place is of knowledge? Knowledge is the comprehension by contemplation of the things holding in the same way; understanding is the discernment. Verse 15. And silver will not be set as an exchange of it. Nothing is of equal worth to wisdom. If more simply you understand the silver and the gold, at once Job will say that nothing is worthy of wisdom. Verse 16. In precious onyx and sapphire. Not even to precious onyx will wisdom be compared; but neither in sapphire will it be equalled. Verse 18. Lofty things and gabis will not be remembered. Neither the lofty things are worthy of wisdom, nor gabis. It seems to be set upon powerful things, as it were gigartic (corrupt word; perhaps gigantic) ones. But some say that gabis is called the thing standing above the lip of the medimnus, which is called cumulatum (the heaped part). Verse 18. And draw wisdom above the innermost things. The innermost things around India, or the things around the country beyond, where there are precious stones. And that country brings these things to men, being thought among the rich to be marvellous. Beyond those innermost things then draw wisdom into yourself. Or, above the innermost things, the more than unspeakable inner mysteries, the holy things of God; above all things, being many, draw wisdom. Verse 21. It has escaped every man. It has escaped every man, even if he is a prophet, even if an apostle. Chapter 29, verse 6 (numeral lost). When my ways were being poured with butter. We have said before about the ways of Job, which he walked, that they were virtues. So his ways were poured with butter, he walked temperance, and as it were temperance was being poured, so that many, also of the infants, were nourished from the temperance of Job, from the righteousness of Job, from the courage. For this is: When my ways were poured with butter. Verse 6 (numeral lost). And my mountains were poured with milk. As many as were high and great thoughts, these were Job's mountains, upon which he went up. Verse 7. When I went out upright in a city. He was at leisure for teaching and benefit, loving, not as self-loving, but as having love seeking the common advantage. Verse 9. Placing a finger upon a mouth. It will seem then also to be a sign, the 'placing a finger upon their mouth', of silence. But perhaps it shows, since the hand is taken instead of works, as we have often shown, that they placed their work upon the mouth, having perceived, in little work, that they are not worthy of speaking, Job being present, having done greater works. Verse 10. And those having heard called me blessed. Of the same. So much was he when not yet he was being tortured, that those hearing him called him blessed, and wondered in what way he understands and grasps such great things, and is able to benefit the hearers. Verse 10. For their tongue was glued to their throat. Of those hearing me and calling me blessed upon the things I was saying, the tongue was glued to the throat. Verse 11. For an ear heard, and called me blessed. Of the same. Just as it has been written about Moses, that he was wary of looking at before God through the excess of his brightness; thus one would understand that there was an excess of progress of Job's in wisdom, so that those hearing him are not able to look into the sparkle of his thoughts, and not being able because of this to turn aside their eyes, not following the deepest of his mind. Because of this he says: Verse 11. But an eye having seen me turned aside. Aquila and Symmachus have given out: it testified about me; but others: but an eye having seen turned aside, instead of: I am not strong to speak against. Verse 12. For I saved a poor man out of a hand of a powerful one. Let us see his brave deeds, and let us unfold them. pass_b_english: … you have been stirred up to provoke me. I swear to you, and I swear by the living Lord himself, who judged that I should suffer these things, the very one who handed me over to these straits, who gave the devil authority to have me tested and tortured with such trials. I swear by the Lord, and I say: “The Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul” (Job 27:2).

“Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die” (Job 27:5). If we were to agree with what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would have declared you righteous until I die.
“For I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). I will not stop giving heed to righteousness; I will remember always to hold fast to it.

“For I am not conscious of having done anything out of place” (Job 27:6). His freedom of speech is great, both about his earlier life and about what he did in the time of his trouble, so that he can say: “I am not conscious of having done anything out of place.”
“But what is the place of knowledge?” (Job 28:12). Knowledge is the grasp in contemplation of things that always stay the same; understanding is discernment.

“And silver will not be weighed out in exchange for it” (Job 28:15). Nothing is worth as much as wisdom. If you take the silver and the gold in the simpler sense, Job will at once be saying that nothing is worthy of wisdom.
“With precious onyx and sapphire” (Job 28:16). Wisdom will not be compared even with precious onyx; no, nor will it be made equal to a sapphire.

“Lofty things and gabis will not be mentioned” (Job 28:18). Neither lofty things nor gabis are worthy of wisdom. It seems to be set down of things that are mighty, as it were [gigantic]. But some say that “gabis” is the name for what stands up above the rim of a medimnus, which is called the heaped measure.

“And draw wisdom above the innermost things” (Job 28:18). The innermost things are those around India, or those in the country beyond it, where precious stones are found. That country yields these things to people, and among the rich they are thought marvellous. So beyond those innermost things, draw wisdom into yourself. Or else, “above the innermost things”: the holy mysteries of God within, which are beyond all telling. Above all things, many as they are, draw wisdom.
“It has escaped every human being” (Job 28:21). It has escaped every human being, even if he is a prophet, even if he is an apostle.

“When my paths were flowing with butter” (Job 29:6). We have said before about the paths Job walked, that they were virtues. So his paths flowed with butter: he walked in self-control, and his self-control flowed out, as it were, so that many, even of the little ones, were fed by Job's self-control, by Job's righteousness, by his courage. That is the meaning of “When my paths were flowing with butter.”
“And my mountains were flowing with milk” (Job 29:6). Whatever thoughts were high and great, these were Job's mountains, and he climbed up onto them.
“When I went out upright in the city” (Job 29:7). He gave his time to teaching and to doing good, out of love: not as a lover of himself, but as one who had a love that seeks the common good.

“Laying a finger on their mouth” (Job 29:9). It will seem that “laying a finger on their mouth” is a sign of silence. But perhaps, since the hand is taken for works, as we have often shown, it shows that they laid their work on their mouth: they perceived, being slight in work, that they were not worthy to speak while Job was present, who had done greater works.
“And those who heard me called me blessed” (Job 29:10).

From the same: So great was he, when he was not yet being tormented, that those who heard him called him blessed and wondered how he could understand and grasp so many things and was able to help those who heard him.
“For their tongue stuck to their throat” (Job 29:10). The tongue of those who heard me, and who called me blessed for what I said, stuck to their throat.
“For the ear heard and called me blessed” (Job 29:11).

From the same: It is written of Moses that he was afraid to look upon God because of the surpassing greatness of his brightness (Exodus 3:6). In the same way one might understand that Job's progress in wisdom was so surpassing that those who heard him could not look into the brilliance of his thoughts; and because they could not, they turned their eyes aside, unable to follow the great depth of his mind. That is why he says: “But the eye that saw me turned aside” (Job 29:11). Aquila and Symmachus have rendered it “It bore witness about me”; others, “But the eye that saw turned aside,” meaning: I am not strong enough to speak against him.

“For I rescued a poor man from the hand of the powerful” (Job 29:12). Let us look at his brave deeds and unfold them. This saying has a meaning according to the letter, and by way of anagogy it has an interpretation much more. According to the …
